label: Proposition D
title: Changes to Ballot Measure Process
q: Shall the City amend the Charter to increase the requirements for signature initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters in San Francisco (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements for calling special elections, allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn before an election, and remove the ability of a minority of Board of Supervisors members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot?
now:
The San Francisco Board of Supervisors (Board) has 11 members. A measure can be either an ordinance to change the law or a declaration of policy. Under the City Charter, measures can be placed on the ballot in several ways, including:
• By a majority vote of the Board;
• By four or more Board members without a Board vote;
• By the Mayor without a Board vote; or
• By a signature initiative (petition) signed by at least 2% of the registered voters in San Francisco, currently about 10,600 signatures. Currently San Francisco has over 530,000 registered voters. Signature initiatives usually appear on the ballot at the next regularly scheduled election. Signature initiatives may call for an earlier “special” election on an ordinance if the petition is signed by at least 10% of the votes cast for all candidates for Mayor in the last election. Currently, this is about 39,000 signatures. Once a signature initiative is submitted to the Department of Elections, it cannot be withdrawn.${F(1)}
does:
Proposition D would amend the Charter to increase the requirements to put measures on the ballot by:
• Increasing the number of signatures required to place a signature initiative on the ballot from 2% to 8% (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures) of the registered voters in San Francisco.${F(1)}
yes: If you vote “yes,” you want to increase the requirements for signature initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements for special elections, allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn, and remove the ability of a minority of Board members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot.
no: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.

1: Official Voter Information Guide, San Francisco, Nov. 3, 2026, p. 84
